Under the standard composition convention (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) used by the source wiki, f \circ f^{-1} is the identity on T, not on S, so the two identity subscripts are swapped: the first composite is I_{\powerset T} and the second is I_{\powerset S}.
source_fields.problem:
Title: Inverse of Direct Image Mapping is Direct Image Mapping of Inverse

Let $S$ and $T$ be [[Definition:Set|sets]].

Let $f :S \to T$ be a [[Definition:Bijection|bijection]].

Let $f^\to$ be the [[Definition:Direct Image Mapping of Mapping|direct image mapping]] of $f$.

Then:
:$\paren {f^\to}^{-1} = \paren {f^{-1} }^{\to}$
where $f^{-1}$ and $\paren{f^\to}^{-1}$ denote the [[Definition:Inverse of Mapping|inverses]] of $f$ and $f^\to$ respectively
source_fields.witness:
Take S = {0}, T = {1} (disjoint one-element sets) and the bijection f : S -> T given by f = {0 |-> 1}, so f^{-1} : T -> S is {1 |-> 0}. Under the source wiki's convention (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)):

  f o f^{-1} : T -> T has graph {1 |-> 1}, i.e. domain {1} = T. So f o f^{-1} = I_T, NOT I_S. The point 1 lies in the domain of the composite but not in the domain of I_S (= {0}), so I_S is not even defined at 1; comparing mappings as (domain, codomain, graph) triples, f o f^{-1} != I_S.

  Lifting to direct image mappings: f^-> : P(S) -> P(T) and (f^{-1})^-> : P(T) -> P(S), so the composite f^-> o (f^{-1})^-> has domain P(T) = {{}, {1}} and graph {{} |-> {}, {1} |-> {1}}. That is I_{P(T)}. The proof's displayed line asserts it equals I_{P(S)}, which has domain P(S) = {{}, {0}} and is undefined at the subset {1}.

  Symmetrically, f^{-1} o f has graph {0 |-> 0} with domain {0} = S, so it equals I_S and (f^{-1})^-> o f^-> = I_{P(S)}, whereas the proof writes I_T / I_{P(T)}.

For this singleton witness, the correct identities are f∘f⁻¹=I_T and f⁻¹∘f=I_S. The selected Lean declarations verify the bijection and distinguish the composite graph and its direct image from the printed identity on S. The counterexample concerns the swapped subscripts in the proof, not the final inverse-of-direct-image theorem.

Title: Characterization of Natural Transformation Between Bifunctors

Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be [[Definition:Category|categories]].

:$F \tuple{C, -}$ and $G \tuple{C, -}$
denote the [[Definition:Functor|functors]] obtained by [[Definition:Bifunctor|substituting the first variable]] of $F$ and $G$, respectively, with $C$.

For each [[Definition:Object (Category Theory)|object]] $D \in\mathbf D$ let:
:$F \tuple{-, D}$ and $G \tuple{-, D}$

Title: Image of Frame under Frame Homomorphism is Frame/Corollary

Let $L_1 = \struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ be [[Definition:Frame (Lattice Theory)|frames]].

:$S_3$ denotes the [[Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping|image]] of $S_1$ under $\phi$
:$\preceq_3$ denotes the [[Definition:Restricted Ordering|restricted ordering]] of $\preceq_2$ to the [[Definition:Subset|subset]] $S_3$.

Then:

Its restriction to S₁×S₃ is unchanged. φ preserves top, finite meets, and all joins, so it is a frame homomorphism. Take A={0,1}. Then ∨₁A=1 and φ[A]={0,1}. The meet of phi[A]={0,1} is 0. By the definition of [[Definition:Content of Rational Polynomial|content]], and using that $a \in \Z$:
:$\cont {b n q f} = a \cont {n f}$
source_fields.explanation:
The challenged integral-scalar content step permits negative integera; normalization of content is nonnegative. Keep a=-1,b=n=2,q=-1/2,f=X+1, henceg=nf=2X+2 andbnqf=-g. Both contents are2, whilea*contentg=-2. Actual integer Polynomial.content; monicity establishescontent(X+1)=1, and content_C_mul computescontentg andcontent(-g).

Content is defined as a gcd of coefficients (nonnegative by the standard gcd convention) and, for nonzero rational polynomials, as the positive rational c with f = c f* and f* primitive; the zero polynomial has content 0. Hence cont(a g) >= 0 always, while a cont(g) < 0 whenever a < 0 and g != 0, so the two sides cannot be equal for any negative scalar. The proof never splits on the sign of a (or b), and the omission propagates verbatim to the last line. The correct identities are cont(a g) = |a| cont(g) and cont(q f) = |q| cont(f).

source_fields.problem:
Title: Closure of Complement of Closure is Regular Closed

Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a [[Definition:Topological Space|topological space]].

Let $A \subseteq S$ be a [[Definition:Subset|subset]] of $T$.

Let $A^-$ denote the [[Definition:Topological Closure|closure]] of $A$ in $T$.

Let $A'$ denote the [[Definition:Relative Complement|complement]] of $A$ in $S$: $A' = S \setminus A$.

Then $A^{-'-}$ is [[Definition:Regular Closed Set|regular closed]].
source_fields.witness: Let X={0,1} with topology {∅,{1},X}. Take A={0} and x=0. The closed sets are ∅,{0},X, so cl(A)={0}. Thus U=X\cl(A)={1}. Since the only closed set containing {1} is X, cl(U)=X, hence int(cl(U))=X. Therefore x∈int(cl(U)) but x∉U.

source_fields.claim_quote:
Let $P_f, P_g, P_\RR$ be the [[Definition:URM Program|URM programs]] computing, respectively, the functions $f$ and $g$ and the [[Definition:Characteristic Function of Relation|characteristic function]] $\chi_\RR$.

From [[Recursive Function is URM Computable]], these programs are guaranteed to exist.
source_fields.explanation:
The complete source permits an arbitrary relation R but asserts existence of a URM program computing its characteristic function. This local assertion is the quoted target. With both branches constant zero, the final function h is recursive; the record does not claim otherwise. Keep the original diagonal relation R(n) iff program n does not halt on input n with output1, and the original total constant-zero branch functions. A supposed characteristic program contradicts its own diagonal case; the explicit zeroing program validates the source premises and supplies a nonvacuous control. The original pairing and four-instruction URM model remain. General pairing and instruction roundtrips, a proved decoder fuel bound, full finite-program roundtrip, and decoder surjectivity connect every finite instruction-list program to its code. Mathlib reflexive transitive closure supplies unbounded finite runs. Deterministic halting uniqueness and the direct all-program nonexistence theorem close the earlier coverage gap.

Thus the claimed program does not exist; the cited theorem applies only when χ_R is recursive.

Separate mathematical remark (not part of the selected formal certificate): the theorem as literally stated, with no hypothesis that R has a recursive (URM-computable) characteristic function, is itself false. With f ≡ 1 and g ≡ 0 the function h defined by the theorem would be the characteristic function χ_R, so a relation R whose characteristic function is not recursive (for example the diagonal relation used above) gives a non-recursive h. The selected certificate instantiates f = g = 0 and refutes only the asserted existence of a program computing χ_R for arbitrary R; with that instantiation h is recursive.

source_fields.problem:
Title: Combination of Recursive Functions

Let $f: \N^k \to \N$ and $g: \N^k \to \N$ be [[Definition:Recursive Function|recursive functions]] (not necessarily [[Definition:Total Function|total]]), where $k \ge 1$.

Let $\RR$ be a [[Definition:Relation|$k$-ary relation]] such that:
:if $\map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ holds, then $\map f {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ is defined
:if $\map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ does not hold, then $\map g {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ is defined.

Let $h: \N^k \to \N$ be the [[Definition:Function|function]] defined as:
:$\map h {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} = \begin {cases}
\map f {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} & : \text{if } \map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} \text { holds} \\
\map g {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} & : \text{otherwise}
\end {cases}$
so that $h$ is [[Definition:Total Function|total]].

Then $h$ is [[Definition:Recursive Function|recursive]].
source_fields.witness: Fix an enumeration of URM programs. Define R(n) iff program n, run on input n, does not halt with output 1. This is a relation on naturals, so it satisfies the sole stated condition that R is arbitrary.

source_fields.problem:
Title: Edge is Minimum Weight Bridge iff in All Minimum Spanning Trees

Let $G$ be an [[Definition:Undirected Network|undirected network]].

Let every [[Definition:Edge of Graph|edge]] of $G$ have a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Weight (Network Theory)|weight]].

Let $e$ be an [[Definition:Edge of Graph|edge]] of $G$.

Then $e$ is a [[Definition:Bridge (Graph Theory)|bridge]] of minimum [[Definition:Weight (Network Theory)|weight]] in $G$ {{iff}} $e$ belongs to every [[Definition:Minimum Spanning Tree|minimum spanning tree]] of $G$.
source_fields.witness: Undirected connected triangle with vertices {0,1,2} and weighted edges 01↦1, 12↦2, 02↦3. Let e=01. The three spanning trees are {01,12}, {01,02}, {12,02}, with weights 3, 4, 5. Thus {01,12} is the unique minimum spanning tree, so e belongs to every MST. But deleting e leaves edges 02 and 12, which connect 0–2–1. Hence e is not a bridge and therefore cannot be a minimum-weight bridge.

source_fields.witness:
Two independent explicit witnesses, both verified by exact integer arithmetic (deterministic trial division + the % operator; no floats).

WITNESS 1 (spurious member, interval-independent): n = 139. The proof lists 139 among "the primes of the form 4m + 1". But 139 mod 4 = 3, i.e. 139 = 4*34 + 3. Equivalently, 139 - 1 = 138 and 138 = 4*34 + 2 is not divisible by 4, so there is NO integer m with 4m + 1 = 139. (139 is indeed prime, but it lies in the residue class 3 mod 4, not 1 mod 4.) This witness needs no assumption whatsoever about the intended interval.

WITNESS 1b (the proof's own self-contradiction, mechanically confirmed): 4*35 - 1 = 139 exactly, so the proof's earlier line "139 = 4*35 - 1" places 139 in the class 4m - 1 = 4m + 3. Residue classes 1 and 3 mod 4 are disjoint, so the two lines cannot both hold; the recomputation shows 139 mod 4 = 3, so the listed-as-4m+1 line is the false one.

WITNESS 2 (omitted member): n = 149. 149 is prime (trial division to 12*12 > 149 finds no divisor) and 149 = 4*37 + 1, so 149 mod 4 = 1. Also 118 < 149 < 157, so 149 lies inside the stated range under every reading of the endpoints. It is absent from the asserted list {137, 139, 157}.

Recomputed truth: primes in 119..156 are 127, 131, 137, 139, 149, 151; those ≡ 1 (mod 4) are exactly {137, 149}. On the closed interval [118, 157] they are exactly {137, 149, 157}. Under no reading is the answer {137, 139, 157}.

Concrete "claim says X, here X = Y" form: claim says {p prime in the range : p ≡ 1 mod 4} = {137, 139, 157}; recomputed, that set = {137, 149} (open range 119..156) or {137, 149, 157} (closed range 118..157). 139 ∈ claimed set but 139 mod 4 = 3 ≠ 1; 149 ∈ true set but 149 ∉ claimed set.

source_fields.problem:
Title: Surjection Induced by Powerset is Induced by Surjection

Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a [[Definition:Relation|relation]].

Let $\RR^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ be the [[Definition:Direct Image Mapping of Relation|direct image mapping]] $\RR$.

Let $\RR^\to$ be a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].

Let $X = \Preimg \RR$, that is, the [[Definition:Preimage of Relation|preimage]] of $\RR$.

Then $\RR {\restriction_X} \subseteq X \times T$, that is, the [[Definition:Restriction of Relation|restriction of $\RR$ to $X$]], is a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].
source_fields.witness:
The asserted lemma is FALSE, refuted by a 3-pair relation on a 2-element set; a 4-pair endorelation on a 3-element set refutes BOTH halves at once; and a 4-pair relation with S != T even refutes the downstream "cannot be a surjection" conclusion.

WITNESS 1 (smallest; refutes the sentence as literally written).
  S = T = {0,1},  R = {(0,0), (1,0), (1,1)}, i.e. R(0) = {0}, R(1) = {0,1}.
  Case (2) hypothesis holds: x = 1 is R-related to y_1 = 0 and y_2 = 1, and y_1 != y_2.
  Direct image mapping R^->(A) = union_{x in A} R(x):
    R^->({}) = {},  R^->({0}) = {0},  R^->({1}) = {0,1},  R^->({0,1}) = {0,1}.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {0,1} }.
  Claim says {y_1} = {0} is NOT in Rng(R^->); here A = {0} gives R^->(A) = {0}, so {0} IS in Rng(R^->).

WITNESS 2 (endorelation, refutes BOTH conjuncts simultaneously; hand-verified separately).
  S = T = {0,1,2},  R = {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (2,1)}, i.e. R(0) = {0,1}, R(1) = {0}, R(2) = {1}.
  Case (2) holds: x = 0 branches to y_1 = 0 and y_2 = 1.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {1}, {0,1} }.
  A = {1} gives R^->(A) = {0} = {y_1}; A = {2} gives R^->(A) = {1} = {y_2}.
  Claim says neither singleton can be in the range; here BOTH are.

WITNESS 3 (refutes the CONCLUSION itself when the relation is heterogeneous, S != T).
  S = {0,1,2}, T = {0,1},  R = {(0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (2,1)}: R(0) = {0}, R(1) = {1}, R(2) = {0,1}.
  Case (2) holds: x = 2 branches to y_1 = 0, y_2 = 1.
  Rng(R^->) = { {}, {0}, {1}, {0,1} } = P(T); |Rng(R^->)| = 4 = |P(T)| = 4.
  Claim says R^-> "cannot be a surjection"; here R^-> IS a surjection onto P(T).

source_fields.claim_quote: It can also be shown that this proof works for the general [[Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)|ring]] whether it be a [[Definition:Ring with Unity|ring with unity]] or not.
source_fields.explanation: The final sentence explicitly extends the unchanged proof to rings without unity. The null ring on ℤ/2 is admissible for that extension even though the preceding main statement assumed unity. Over it the full untruncated Cauchy multiplication is identically zero, so no sequence acts as a unit and no square is nonzero; the unit-dependent construction of the displayed proof therefore does not go through as written. This refutes only the literal claim that this same construction/proof works without unity; it does not assert that polynomial rings over non-unital rings cannot be defined or that the isomorphism fails under some other construction, and the theorem proper (ring with unity) is not challenged. No census of small rings is claimed or endorsed.
source_fields.flaw: The closing claim that the same proof works for a general ring, with or without unity. The displayed proof uses the multiplicative identity 1 of R to form the unity ⟨1,0,0,…⟩ of the sequence ring and the element x = ⟨0,1,0,…⟩ with x² = ⟨0,0,1,0,…⟩; in a ring without unity no multiplicative identity is available to play that role, and for the null ring the key computation fails outright.
source_fields.witness: R = the null ring on ℤ/2: the additive group {0, 1} with addition mod 2 and a·b = 0 for all a, b (equivalently 2ℤ/4ℤ). It is a ring in the general sense (associativity and distributivity hold trivially since every product is 0) and has no multiplicative identity (1·1 = 0 ≠ 1), so it is a ring without unity, exactly the case the sentence claims the proof covers. Form the proof's own object S = R^(ℕ), the sequences over R with componentwise addition and Cauchy-product multiplication (f·g)_n = Σ_{i+j=n} f_i g_j, over all infinite sequences (no truncation). Three certified conclusions: (1) every Cauchy product is the zero sequence, since each coefficient is a finite sum of products in R, all zero; (2) S has no left multiplicative identity: for the nonzero constant sequence f = ⟨1,1,1,…⟩ every product u·f is the zero sequence ≠ f, so no sequence u acts as an identity; hence no multiplicative identity is available to play the role of the proof's ⟨1,0,0,…⟩ (that tuple is a well-defined sequence, since the additive element 1 of ℤ/2 exists, but it is not a multiplicative identity); (3) no sequence has a nonzero square, so the proof's key computation x² = ⟨0,0,1,0,…⟩ ≠ 0 for x = ⟨0,1,0,…⟩ fails. The selected Lean theorem certifies exactly these three statements for the NonUnitalCommRing on ZMod 2 with zero multiplication and the full-sequence Cauchy product: (∀ f g, cauchy f g = 0) ∧ ¬(∃ u, ∀ f, cauchy u f = f) ∧ ¬(∃ f, cauchy f f ≠ 0).

source_fields.problem:
Title: Construction of Direct Product of Fields

Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]] whose [[Definition:Field Zero|zero]] is $0$ and whose [[Definition:Multiplicative Identity|multiplicative identity]] is $1$.

Let $E = F \times F$ be the [[Definition:Cartesian Product|Cartesian product]] of $F$ with itself.

Let [[Definition:Field Addition|addition]] be defined on $E$ by:
:$\forall a, b, c, d \in F: \tuple {a, b} +_E \tuple {c, d} := \tuple {a +_F c, b +_F d}$

Let [[Definition:Field Product|multiplication]] be defined on $E$ by:
:$\forall a, b, c, d \in F: \tuple {a, b} \times_E \tuple {c, d} := \tuple {\paren {a \times_F c} +_F \paren {-\paren {b \times_F d} }, \paren {a \times_F d} +_F \paren {b \times_F c} }$

Then $\struct {E, +_E, \times_E}$ is a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]].
source_fields.witness: Let F=F5 and use the printed product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−bd,ad+bc). The nonzero pair u=(1,2) has 1²+2²=0, contradicting the printed criterion. The nonzero pair v=(1,3) satisfies uv=(0,0). Consequently the nonzero elements are not closed under multiplication, and u has no inverse: if uy=1, then v=(uy)v=y(uv)=0, a contradiction. The selected Lean theorem verifies these facts in Mathlib's QuadraticAlgebra (ZMod 5) (-1) 0. This refutes both the local criterion and the unrestricted assertion that the construction always gives a field.

source_fields.problem:
Title: Equivalence of Definitions of Curvature/Whewell Form to Parametric Polar Form

{{TFAE|def = Curvature}}

=== [[Definition:Curvature/Whewell Form|Whewell Form]] ===
The '''[[Definition:Curvature|curvature]]''' $\kappa$ of $C$ at a [[Definition:Point|point]] $P$ can be expressed in the form of a [[Definition:Whewell Equation|Whewell equation]] as:

:$\kappa = \dfrac {\d \psi} {\d s}$
where:
:$\psi$ is the [[Definition:Turning Angle|turning angle]] of $C$
:$s$ is the [[Definition:Arc Length|arc length]] of $C$.
=== [[Definition:Curvature/Parametric Form/Polar|Parametric Polar Form]] ===
Let $C$ be embedded in a [[Definition:Polar Plane|polar plane]] and defined by the [[Definition:Parametric Equation|parametric equations]]:
:$\begin{cases} r = \map r t \\ \theta = \map \theta t \end{cases}$

The '''[[Definition:Curvature|curvature]]''' $\kappa$ of $C$ at a [[Definition:Point|point]] $P = \polar {r, \theta}$ is given by:

:$\kappa = \dfrac {2 r'^2 \theta' + r r' ' \theta' + r r' \theta' ' + r^2 \theta'^3} {\paren {r'^2 + \paren {r \theta'}^2}^{1/2} }$
where:
:$r' = \dfrac {\d r} {\d t}$ is the [[Definition:Derivative|derivative]] of $r$ {{WRT|Differentiation}} $t$ at $P$
:$\theta' = \dfrac {\d \theta} {\d t}$ is the [[Definition:Derivative|derivative]] of $\theta$ {{WRT|Differentiation}} $t$ at $P$
:$r' '$ and $\theta' '$ are the [[Definition:Second Derivative|second derivatives]] of $r$ and $y$ {{WRT|Differentiation}} $t$ at $P$.
source_fields.witness: Take r(t)=1+t and θ(t)=t, with Cartesian curve γ(t)=((1+t)cos t,(1+t)sin t). It is regular since ‖γ′(t)‖²=1+(1+t)²>0. At t=0: r=1, r′=1, r″=0, θ′=1, θ″=0. Near t=0 the radius is positive. At zero the Whewell curvature is (3/2)/sqrt(2)=3/(2sqrt(2)), whereas the printed polar expression is 3/sqrt(2). This witness detects the denominator error; r-second-derivative is zero here, so it does not separately test the sign of that term.
